idiom_name: ObjectSpace::WeakMap (weak keys and values, identity) and ObjectSpace::WeakKeyMap (weak keys, strong values, eql?); legacy WeakRef
implementation_notes: Ruby's core realizes the pattern through the ObjectSpace weak containers: WeakMap compares keys by identity and holds both keys and values weakly, while WeakKeyMap (Ruby 3.3+) compares keys by value with eql?/hash, holds only the keys weakly and keeps values strongly, and is documented for caches of lightweight value objects where unused copies should be collected. The bundled weakref library (WeakRef) is the legacy shim built on WeakMap; it raises WeakRef::RefError when the referent has been collected, so its callers must rescue rather than test - prefer the core classes. Ruby has no per-object weak field: a weak edge lives in one of these containers, or in an object's key role inside one.
pitfalls: WeakMap keys are compared by identity, so an equal-but-distinct object creates a second entry: use WeakKeyMap (or intern the keys) when equality is the intended semantics.

Only garbage-collectable objects are accepted: symbols, Integer/Float and other immediates raise ArgumentError as keys or values, so an integer-keyed cache must key on an object you own or on an explicitly held wrapper.

Nothing notifies the structure that an entry died - the containers simply drop what they hold weakly - so anything kept alongside them (counts, indexes, reverse lookups) must tolerate and periodically reconcile missing entries.
